query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Grain-boundary segregation and precipitation of solute elements in high-entropy alloys lead to a decrease in toughness due to the formation of brittle grain-boundary phases, which can be mitigated by controlling the alloy composition and processing conditions to suppress segregation and precipitation.
generation.intervention: Controlled variation of alloy composition and processing conditions
generation.conditions: High and low temperature, various loading conditions
generation.predicted_outcome: Decrease in toughness by 20% relative to the initial baseline
generation.baseline: Initial toughness of the high-entropy alloy
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 300-1000 K, loading range: 100-1000 MPa
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between grain-boundary segregation and toughness degradation is still unclear, and further research is needed to fully understand the underlying mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of high-entropy alloys with varying compositions and processing conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the toughness of the high-entropy alloy does not decrease by more than 10% relative to the initial baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) contain multiple principal (or major) elements, commonly five or more, in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios, differently from conventional alloys. While the configurational entropy of an alloy increases with the increasing number of alloying elements, multiple principal elements of an HEA lead to high entropy of mixing that thus suppresses the formation of intermetallic compounds [,,]. Therefore, stable solid solution phases, such as face-centered cubic (FCC) phase, body-centered cubic (BCC) phase, and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase can be obtained [,]. Meanwhile, HEAs have been shown to exhibit outstanding mechanical and chemical properties, such as high strength and hardness [,], exceptional ductility, as well as excellent oxidation and corrosion resistances [], and thus have become potential candidate materials for many challenging industrial applications. The design and application of HEAs require a comprehensive understanding of their properties and underlying deformation mechanisms.
